overview: Ngarrindjeri communities connect the lower Murray, lakes, Coorong and Sea Country through law, kinship, food and shared responsibilities. Their cultural life continues despite dispossession and environmental disruption.

items.text: The Tendi is described in the community's Sea Country Plan as a governing council that makes and interprets Ngarrindjeri law.
Freshwater and marine environments supplied fish, shellfish, eels, waterbirds and plants. Stored food supported gatherings for exchange, ceremonies and social life.
Tools included nets, weirs, spears, traps and decoys. Bark canoes, reed rafts and floating fishing platforms supported work on the water.
Ngartji relationships connect people with particular animals and plants, bringing responsibilities to care for them. Ecological knowledge passes between generations.
A mission was established at Point McLeay in 1859, now Raukkan Community. It sheltered some displaced people while missionaries pressed for changes to language and belief.
Elder Ellen Trevorrow teaches weaving and cultural storytelling at Camp Coorong. Workshops connect younger generations and visitors with knowledge through making.
